activities.title: Letters sitting on the line
materials: paper with a line drawn across (or lined paper)
parentPrompts: Draw a thick line across the middle of a sheet. Explain that letters sit on it, like toys on a shelf.
Have your child write the letter T so that it stands on the line, then L and I.
Ask: "Is your letter sitting on the line or floating?" Let them fix any that float.
Look for: letters that start at the top and rest on the line. Tall letters (T, L, I) should be taller than small ones (c, o).

activities.title: Match capital and small letters
parentPrompts: Write capital letters S, A, T, P on 4 cards and small s, a, t, p on 4 other cards.
Lay all cards face up. Have your child match each capital with its small partner and name them.
Ask: "Which pair looks almost the same only in a different size?" (S and s, for example.)
Look for: matches S-s, T-t, A-a, P-p. Then write one partner pair on paper together.

activities.title: Write with finger spaces
materials: a craft stick or a flat sticker
parentPrompts: Say: "Words need space so we can read them." Write 'I see a cat' with no spaces, then with spaces, and read both.
Give your child a craft stick (a 'space stick'). Have them lay it down after each word to keep the space.
Help them write 'I am' and 'I see' using the stick, one word at a time.
Ask: "Where do I put the stick?" Look for: a visible gap between each word they write.

activities.title: Practice a favorite letter
parentPrompts: Let your child choose any letter they have practiced and say why they like it.
Write it big, then medium, then small, in different colors.
Decorate the letter with patterns or stickers. Say its name and a word that starts with its sound.
Look for: they can say the name of the letter and write it from the top.

activities.title: Write my name
parentPrompts: Show the name card. Say each letter name slowly as you point.
Have your child write their name 3 times: once with your help, once copying, once from memory.
Underline the first letter (capital) with a colored crayon.
Ask: "Does every letter sit on the line?" Look for: correct letters in order. Reversed letters are common at age 5; just model the right way gently.

activities.title: Number card game
materials: number cards 1 to 10 (write on paper squares)
parentPrompts: Make cards for 1 to 10, with the numeral. Shuffle and deal each player a few cards.
Each player flips one card at the same time. The bigger number wins both cards.
If they disagree, check by counting out that many items for each card and lining them up.
Look for: they can say which numeral is bigger. Ask: "How do you know?" Counting up to the number is a fine answer.

activities.title: Sort objects and count each group
materials: a pile of mixed small things (socks, toy cars, buttons)
parentPrompts: Keep small items like buttons, coins, and seeds out of mouths, and stay close while your child plays.
Mix up a pile of 10 to 15 things that can be sorted, like blocks of different colors.
Ask your child to sort them into groups. Ask: "How did you sort them?"
Count each group and say the number. Ask: "Which group has the most? Which has the fewest?"
Look for: a clear rule for each group (color, size or kind) and correct counts. Try sorting a new way afterward.

activities.title: Join two groups
parentPrompts: Put 2 cars in a parking spot. Drive 1 more in. Ask: "How many cars are there now?" Count them.
Say it as a story: "2 and 1 more makes 3." Try 1 and 3, then 2 and 2.
Write the math on paper for your child: 2 + 1 = 3. Say what the plus and equals signs mean: 'and' and 'makes'.
Look for: they can say how many in all by counting. Using fingers is great.

activities.title: Show numbers on fingers
parentPrompts: Show 2 fingers on one hand and 1 on the other. Ask: "How many fingers in all?"
Take turns calling out two small numbers for each other to show and add.
Play 'Show me 5': you hold up some fingers and ask how many more to make 5.
Look for: they can show each number and count the total. Over time they will know some facts without counting.

activities.title: Act out math stories
materials: toy animals or other small toys
parentPrompts: Tell a short story and act it out: "3 ducks are swimming. 2 more come. How many ducks now?"
Have your child act out the story with toys and count the answer.
Switch: let them tell you a story and you solve it. Keep numbers to 5 or less.
Look for: they can tell the story with the toys, and give the total. Ask: "How did you find out?"

activities.title: Find the topic of a nonfiction book
materials: a nonfiction (informational) picture book about an animal, plant or weather
parentPrompts: Say: "Some books tell stories and some tell facts about the real world." Show the cover and ask: "What is this book about?"
Read a few pages. After each, ask: "What did we learn?"
At the end say: "The topic is what the whole book is about." Ask your child to say the topic in a few words.
Look for: they can name the topic (like 'ducks' or 'rain') and one fact.

activities.title: Ask and answer questions about facts
parentPrompts: Read a page of the nonfiction book and ask: "What is one fact?"
Ask a question about the page, like "What does this animal eat?" or "Where does it live?" and search the pictures and words to find the answer together.
Draw one fact together and write a short label.
Look for: they can answer with a fact from the book, not only from memory. If they guess, say: "Let's check the book."

activities.title: How pictures help us learn
materials: a nonfiction book with photos or labeled drawings
parentPrompts: Point to a photo and ask: "What is this? How does it help us understand the words?"
Find a picture with labels or arrows. Read the label and point to the part.
Ask your child to find a picture and tell what part of the text it matches.
Look for: they can say what a picture shows and match it to words.

activities.title: Wonder about new words
materials: any picture book with a few interesting words
parentPrompts: Read the book. When you come to a word that may be new, stop and say: "I wonder what that word means."
Look at the picture for clues. Ask: "What do you think it means?" Then tell the meaning in simple words.
Put a sticky note on that page. After reading, act out or draw the new words.
Look for: they notice a new word and ask about it. Using the new word later in the day is a great sign.

activities.title: Compare two books
materials: two books on the same topic (such as animals, plants or weather)
parentPrompts: Look at the covers and the pictures of both books. Say what the topic is.
Read a little from each. Ask: "What is the same? What is different?" (for example, photos vs. drawings).
Draw a line down a paper. Draw one thing from each book on each side.
Look for: they can name at least one way the books are alike or different.

activities.title: Sun and shade feel test
materials: 2 identical objects, like 2 sheets of paper or 2 rocks
a sunny spot and a shady spot
parentPrompts: Safety: never look at the sun. Use sunscreen and a hat if needed. Do not use metal, which can get hot.
Put one object in the sun and one in the shade. Wait about 15 minutes.
Feel each with the back of the hand. Ask: "Which feels warmer? Why do you think so?"
Look for: they say the one in the sun is warmer. Say: "Sunlight warms the surface it shines on."

activities.title: Ice in the sun and in the shade
materials: a sunny spot and a shady spot
parentPrompts: Put one ice cube on a plate in the sun and one in the shade. Ask: "Which will melt faster? Why?"
Check every 5 minutes. Say what you see.
When one is gone, compare the two. The one in the sun should melt faster.
Look for: they connect the sun's warmth to the faster melting. If it is cloudy, try a warm spot (like a window with sunshine) and a cool spot.

activities.title: Design a shade for an ice cube
parentPrompts: Say: "Let's make something to keep an ice cube cool in the sun." Look at the materials and choose what might work.
Build a small shade over one ice cube and leave the other uncovered. Tape if needed.
Check after 10 to 15 minutes. Ask: "Which melted more? Did the shade help?"
Look for: they use a material for shade and say what they saw. Different materials may work differently; try again with another one.

activities.title: Fair play
materials: a simple game or a ball
parentPrompts: Play a game where you take turns. Say: "A fair rule is one that is good for everybody."
Ask: "What if one person always goes first? Is that fair? How can we choose?" Try 'one, two, three' or 'who is oldest'.
Ask: "How does it feel to wait? What can we do while we wait?"
Look for: they can say how to be fair and use turn-taking words.

activities.title: Kind things we can do
parentPrompts: Ask: "What is a neighbor?" (someone who lives or works near us).
Think of kind things to do for a neighbor: say hello, help carry something, share, be quiet at night.
Choose one to do this week. Draw a picture of it.
Look for: they can name a kind act. Include family, friends or pets as neighbors too.

activities.title: Trace a shadow
parentPrompts: Place a toy in the sun so it casts a shadow. Safety: do not look at the sun.
Trace the shadow's outline with chalk or marker on paper or pavement.
Come back later and see how the shadow moved.
Look for: they notice shadows change. Ask: "Why do you think it moved?"

activities.title: Cloud and sun art
parentPrompts: Make a cloud by gluing cotton balls to a plate or paper. Make a sun from yellow paper.
Add raindrops from blue paper.
Hang them with string.
Look for: they link each piece to a kind of weather. Keep glue away from mouths.

activities.title: Move to music
materials: music from a device or sing
parentPrompts: Play music or sing. Move a scarf high and low, fast and slow.
Make the scarf be rain, wind or a bird.
Freeze when the music stops.
Look for: they change their movement with the music.

activities.title: Color and water art
parentPrompts: Fill the jar with water. Add a cloud of shaving cream on top. Do not eat it.
Drop food coloring on the cloud and watch it drip down like rain.
Draw what you saw.
Look for: they can describe what happened. Adult sets up the jar; wash hands after.

activities.title: Fingerprint numbers
parentPrompts: Write a numeral on the paper. Make that many fingerprints next to it.
Do numerals 1 to 5.
Turn the prints into bugs by adding legs.
Look for: the right number of prints for each numeral.
